ABSTRACT
3D object detection leverages sensors like LiDAR and cameras to capture scene information, enabling precise determination of 
objects' spatial positions and orientations. This technology finds extensive applications in autonomous driving, smart homes, in-
dustrial automation, and intelligent security systems. However, high-­precision 3D object detection algorithms often require sub-
stantial computational resources, posing limitations for deployment on resource-­constrained devices. In this paper, we devise an 
efficient computation offloading and data transmission framework specifically tailored for edge computing networks to address 
this challenge. Our framework takes into account both the computing and communication capabilities of terminal devices and 
network conditions, offloading suitable computation tasks to the edge for processing. This approach mitigates the algorithm's 
performance requirements on terminal devices. Furthermore, we propose a data transmission scheme that incorporates atten-
tion mechanisms and hardware-­accelerated coding. This scheme effectively reduces detection time and enhances overall system 
performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly enhances the efficiency of 3D object 
detection on resource-­constrained devices within edge computing networks, while maintaining high detection accuracy.
1   |   Introduction
3D object detection technology [1] involves the utilization of 
sensors, such as lidar and cameras, by terminal devices (e.g., ro-
bots, vehicles) to gather scene information. This process enables 
the detection of objects within the scene and the determination 
of their spatial positions and orientations. This technology has 
found widespread application in autonomous driving, smart 
homes, industrial automation, and intelligent security. For ex-
ample, in autonomous driving, 3D object detection aids in ac-
curately identifying obstacles, locating and categorizing other 
vehicles, and facilitating effective path planning and motion 
prediction to ensure safe vehicle operation [2]. In the context 
of smart home control, it enables intelligent devices like robotic 
vacuum cleaners to recognize various objects and perform pre-
cise interactive operations [3]. Additionally, in security mon-
itoring, it allows for real-­time surveillance of intrusion and 
abnormal activities.
3D object detection algorithms can utilize lidar or cameras for 
environmental data collection. Stereo cameras, due to their 
cost-­effectiveness and flexibility, have emerged as a mainstream

vision algorithms, achieving accurate 3D object detection re-

often results in issues such as limited equipment mobility, high 
energy consumption, and elevated costs, hindering the technol-

With the advancement of technologies like the Internet of Things 
(IoT), edge computing and communication [4], and cloud com-
puting, computation offloading [5, 6] has emerged as a viable 
solution to address the trade-­off between terminal hardware 
performance and cost. By distributing the computational tasks 
required for algorithm execution across terminal and edge de-
vices (or cloud platforms) for collaborative processing, the bur-
den on terminal devices is significantly reduced. This enables 
the deployment of complex algorithms on low-­cost terminal de-
vices. Nonetheless, most existing offloading strategies primar-
ily focus on task allocation efficiency, neglecting the specific 
characteristics of computer vision algorithms, rendering them 
inapplicable. Therefore, this paper aims to design an efficient 
offloading mechanism and data transmission strategy tailored 
for edge computing networks, assisting resource-­constrained 
terminal devices in achieving real-­time and accurate 3D object 
detection.
To accomplish these objectives, several key challenges must be 
addressed:
•	 Given the limited computational resources of terminal 
devices in edge computing networks, executing com-
plex artificial algorithm such as 3D object detection inde-
pendently is challenging. This paper focuses on developing 
a computation offloading scheme that considers both ter-
minal device performance and the 3D object detection algo-
rithm's architecture to ensure efficient detection.
•	 The offloading mechanism involves data transmission be-
tween terminal and edge devices (or cloud platforms) for 
collaborative computing. A crucial challenge is designing 
a transmission scheme that accounts for factors such as the 
algorithm's workflow, hardware performance, and network 
environment, ensuring efficient and accurate data transfer.
•	 Most computation offloading strategies for edge computing 
and communication lack rigorous testing on real hardware, 
particularly for computer vision tasks. This paper bridges 
this gap by validating our offloading approach on actual 
edge devices, proving its effectiveness and efficiency in 
practice.
To tackle these challenges, this paper introduces a tailored com-
putation offloading and data transmission strategy for 3D object 
detection, with the overall process illustrated in Figure 1. After 
collecting environmental information, the terminal device se-
lects an appropriate offloading scheme based on its capabilities, 
executing a portion of the tasks locally. Subsequently, it utilizes 
the proposed efficient data transmission scheme to process, 
encapsulate, and upload the necessary data to edge devices or 
cloud platforms. Upon completion of the remaining tasks by the 
edge server or cloud platform, the detection results are transmit-
ted back to the terminal device for further analysis and use. The 
detailed contributions of this paper are as follows:
•	 Designed a tailored 3D object detection strategy for terminal 
devices with limited computational resources in edge com-
puting networks, which fully considers the performance

2   |   Related Work
2.1   |   3D Object Detection
3D object detection algorithms gather environmental data using 
either lidar or cameras. In various scenarios, stereo cameras have 
become a popular choice because of their cost-­effectiveness and 
versatility. Stereo object detection denotes the task of detecting 
objects utilizing stereo images captured by a pair of left and right 
cameras. In recent years, extensive research has been conducted 
in this domain to enhance the accuracy of object detection in ste-
reo imagery. In 2019, Li et al. [7] introduced Stereo RCNN, a 3D 
object detection method specifically designed for autonomous 
driving and has gained significant attention and popularity in 
the field. To acquire the projection of 3D bounding box verti-
ces within the Region of Interest (RoI) of the left image, stereo 
RCNN incorporates a streamlined keypoint detection network. 
Also in 2019, Qin et al. [8] presented a two-­stage approach based 
on 3D anchor boxes, which explicitly establishes object-­level 
correspondences between regions of interest in stereo images. 
In 2021, Shi et al. [9] proposed StereoCenterNet, a single-­stage, 
anchor-­free stereo detection method inspired by Stereo RCNN 
and similar to CenterNet, thus reducing computation.
Current 3D object detection algorithms often prioritize accu-
racy, neglecting the fact that they require significant computa-
tional resources and memory, thus rendering them unsuitable 
for resource-­constrained terminal devices.
2.2   |   Computation Offloading
Computation offloading stands as a pivotal technology in mo-
bile edge computing (MEC) and communication, vehicular 
networks, and IoT [10–12], enabling resource-­constrained IoT 
devices to tackle intricate computational tasks. Zhao et al. [13] 
introduced a collaborative framework that integrates MEC and 
cloud computing to offload services to vehicles within vehicu-
lar networks, thereby enhancing system utility and diminishing 
computation time. Yang et al. [14] proposed an energy-­efficient 
computation offloading and resource allocation algorithm for 
vehicular edge networks, aiming to minimize the system cost 
under delay constraints using modified particle swarm optimi-
zation. Lang et al. [15] proposed a cooperative computation off-
loading approach in blockchain-­based vehicular edge computing 
networks. It designs a secure data sharing architecture and con-
sensus mechanism and employs game theory to achieve optimal 
offloading decisions, enhancing system security and efficiency. 
These kinds of work focus on universal computation offloading 
strategies; however, they do not consider the complexity of arti-
ficial intelligence algorithms like 3D object detection.
Xie et al. [16] offloaded part of the computing task to an edge 
server to achieve timely image segmentation. Li et al. [17] ad-
opted a point cloud registration strategy, assisted by partial com-
putation offloading, to accomplish the SLAM (Simultaneous 
Localization and Mapping) task for multiple robots. In these 
studies, sophisticated artificial algorithms are deployed across 
terminal devices and edge servers, where devices gather and 
preprocess data, while edge servers handle the primary compu-
tational tasks. However, 3D object detection models are much 
more resource-­intensive than above strategies. Consequently, 
it is essential to implement specific strategies to process data 
during the inference process, ensuring successful deployment of 
the model. Noguchi et al. [18] used split computing for 3D point 
cloud object detection on edge devices, reducing computation 
load and inference time. However, it notes increased data trans-
mission size when splitting within the network, highlighting a 
potential drawback.
2.3   |   Video Encoding
Almost all stereo object detection algorithms use convolutional 
neural networks [19] as the backbone to extract features from 
images and obtain final detection results through an approxi-
mate linear process. If we directly transfer feature maps to the 
servers, it will definitely result in increased transmission latency 
and bandwidth usage. Inspired by video coding technology, this 
paper tries to treat feature maps as video frames and use video 
coding or video compression methods [20] to facilitate efficient 
data transmission.
Relying solely on software for video coding can lead to signifi-
cant consumption of computing resources. Hardware accelera-
tion is a common solution for terminal devices, and this paper 
focuses on hardware encoding acceleration to enhance video 
generation speed. High-­performance edge devices, such as the 
Jetson TX2 [21], offer various video encoding methods, includ-
ing H.264, H.265, and AV1. Furthermore, they support multi-
media processing frameworks like GStreamer [22] and FFmpeg 
[23], all of which can be leveraged for hardware encoding ac-
celeration of videos. However, how to select proper parameters 
used in video coding according to the complex 3D object detec-
tion algorithm remains to be researched deeply.

3.1   |   3D Object Detection Model
The 3D object detection algorithm leverages two images cap-
tured by sensors as inputs to ascertain the object's orientation 
within 3D space through a meticulous series of processing steps. 
While numerous stereo 3D object detection models have been 
devised by researchers, this paper centers on the classic Stereo 
RCNN algorithm [7]. Stereo RCNN utilizes a classic siamese 
network to detect and locate objects in 3D space using paired 
images from stereo cameras, which processes the input data 
through multiple convolutional layers in a feedforward manner 
and outputs the detected 3D object results. Therefore, Stereo 
RCNN can be abstractly represented as a directed acyclic graph 
G, as illustrated in Figure  2. G is mathematically denoted by 
G = ⟨B ∪{enleft, enright, ex}, D⟩. For the sake of clarity and sim-
plicity, the siamese network is consolidated here, and the ensu-
ing algorithm is streamlined accordingly.
Within this framework, B = {b1, b2, … , bn} signifies the var-
ious computational modules constituting the model. These 
modules are determined by the backbone network employed by 
Stereo RCNN, such as ResNet-­34, ResNet-­50, and ResNet-­101 
[24]. In this paper, ResNet-­101 is utilized as the backbone net-
work, resulting in six modules encapsulated within Figure 2. 
According to our previous research [16], the offloading point 
should be selected after the downsampling layers of the back-
bone network, which play the role of feature abstraction to 
reduce the spatial sizes of feature maps. Therefore, this paper 
uses B = {b1, b2, b3, b4, b5} to represent the five sequential con-
volutional modules of ResNet-­101 and use b6 to denote the re-
maining components of the Stereo RCNN network following 
ResNet-­101, encompassing the Stereo RPN, Stereo RCNN, 3D 
Box Estimation, and Dense 3D Box Alignment. The directed 
edges di,j = (bi, bj) ∈D symbolize the transmission connections 
between computational modules, where the output of bi is the 
input of bj. The nodes enleft and enright represent the left and right 
entry points, respectively, and ex denotes the exit node. Among 
these, den,1 signifies the input of the left and right images into 
the ResNet-­101 network, d7,ex represents the final processed out-
come, and the intervening di,j correspond to feature maps with 
dimensions H ∗W ∗C.
3.2   |   Collaborative Detection Model
Given the limited computational resources of terminal devices, 
executing complex 3D object detection algorithms is challeng-
ing. To address this issue, this paper introduces edge servers 
with robust computational capabilities and ample power supply 
to aid in task execution. As previously mentioned, the 3D ob-
ject detection algorithm can be represented as a directed acyclic 
graph, indicating a layered model. Consequently, the aim of this 
paper is to identify an optimal point O in the graph G to serve as 
the computation offloading point. Tasks preceding point O are 
handled by the terminal device, while those following point O 
are processed by the edge computing server, thereby maximiz-
ing system efficiency.
For any given transmission link di,j, there exists a transmis-
sion mode indicator denoted as ci,j. Specifically, ci,j = 0 signifies 
intra-­device transmission, whereas ci,j = 1 indicates transmis-
sion between the device and the edge computing server, mark-
ing the computation offloading point. Notably, if all ci,j values 
are zero, it implies that all computations are executed locally 
on the device. Conversely, the presence of cen,1 = 1 signifies 
that all computations are handled by the edge server, indicat-
ing complete offloading. By identifying the computation off-
loading point, the network can be segmented into two distinct 
parts: the device processing segment and the edge computing 
server processing segment. Here, Bd = {b1, b2, … , bi} ⊂B rep-
resents the computations executed on the terminal device, while 
Be = {bj, … , bn} ⊂B denotes the computations handled by the 
edge server.
3.3   |   Data Transmission Model
At the offloading point, the 3D object detection algorithm pro-
duces a substantial number of feature maps, which are sub-
sequently utilized by the feature extraction network. Direct 
transmission of these feature map data would not only consume 
considerable network bandwidth but also adversely affect the 
system's processing timeliness due to increased transmission 
latency. To mitigate this issue, this paper employs a two-­step ap-
proach to compress the data being transmitted.
Firstly, the paper introduces a channel attention mechanism 
[25] to the original 3D detection model. The channel atten-
tion mechanism, a widely used technique in computer vision,

3.4   |   Detection Time Model
In our proposed model, the overall detection time is funda-
mentally structured around three primary components: the 
processing time of the terminal device, the time required for 
data transmission, and the processing time of the edge server. 
To elaborate, when the data compression duration is designated

This paper strives to minimize detection time by strategically

threshold, and video encoding compression ratio, while main-

4   |   Edge-­Assisted Stereo Object Detection Method
This paper introduces a novel approach tailored for resource-­
constrained terminal devices to achieve real-­time and efficient 
3D object detection within the context of edge computing net-
works. Initially, we identify appropriate locations within the net-
work, denoted as G, to serve as candidate computation offloading 
points. This step aims to alleviate the computational burden on 
the terminal device. Subsequently, input images are extracted 
into a defined number of feature maps. Next, channel attention 
mechanism is employed to process these feature maps. By set-
ting adequate thresholds, we can retain feature maps rich in in-
formation while discarding those with lesser significance, thus 
diminishing the data transmission size. Following this, based 
on the size of the retained feature maps and the video encoding 
capabilities of the terminal hardware, an automated selection 
process is implemented to determine the most suitable feature 
map encoding strategy. These encoded feature maps are then 
encoded into video frames. Leveraging the device's hardware-­
accelerated video encoding and video streaming transmission 
protocols, the video frames are encoded and transmitted in real-­
time to the edge server. Upon receipt, the edge server decodes 
and processes the video stream, subsequently feeding back the 
computed 3D object detection results to the terminal device. The 
detailed solutions for each step are outlined as follows.
4.1   |   Computation Offload Point Selection
3D object detection is a computationally intensive task that re-
quires substantial processing power. Initial tests on the Jetson 
TX2 [26], a high-­performance edge computing device, revealed 
that executing a single 3D detection task takes over 5 s without 
external computational assistance. Clearly, relying solely on the 
terminal device is insufficient for achieving real-­time 3D object 
detection. In this paper, we employ the Stereo RCNN stereo 3D 
detection algorithm, which uses ResNet-­101 as its backbone net-
work. As the input image progresses through the convolutional 
layers of ResNet-­101, it is gradually transformed into abstract 
feature maps that serve as inputs for subsequent processing 
stages. Exploiting this characteristic, we can select a specific 
output point from one of the convolutional blocks to serve as the 
computation offloading point. By processing the feature maps 
generated by these convolutional layers, we can further com-
press and transmit the data.
The selection of the computation offloading point primarily de-
pends on the hardware's performance and the available network 
bandwidth. In practical applications, the point that minimizes 
the overall system latency should be chosen, thereby satisfy-
ing the constraints outlined in  (6). This strategic offloading 
approach allows us to leverage the computational resources of 
edge servers, enabling real-­time 3D object detection on resource-­
constrained terminal devices.

4.2   |   Feature Map Selection
Computational offloading, which entails transmitting data 
between terminal devices and edge servers, necessitates ef-
ficient data compression to minimize transmission latency 
and bandwidth usage. Directly sending the raw feature maps 
generated by the convolutional layers would lead to signifi-
cant delays due to the large data volume. To address this issue, 
our paper incorporates the channel attention mechanism, a 
technique commonly utilized in computer vision algorithms. 
The channel attention mechanism allows us to filter the fea-
ture maps by removing channels with lower attention weights. 
These channels have a minimal impact on the algorithm's ac-
curacy, and their removal results in a reduced data volume. 
By dynamically adjusting the attention score threshold, we 
can tailor the offloading process to different hardware con-
figurations and network conditions, ensuring efficient data 
transmission. After removal process, the leftover feature 
maps from the two branches of the Stereo RCNN model will 
be joined together. As a result, a combined feature map of size 
H ∗W ∗Cf will be produced, where Cf represents the total 
number of channels from the remaining feature maps. And 
the indexes of Cf will be recorded and transferred to the edge 
server for decoding process.
4.3   |   Feature Map Encoding
After completing the feature map selection for the left and right 
branches of the stereo 3D object detection network, this paper 
proceeds to combine the resultant feature maps for subsequent 
processing stages. Nonetheless, the direct transmission of these 
feature maps would entail an excessively large volume of data, 
leading to increased network bandwidth utilization and elevated 
system processing latency. Consequently, additional processing 
is necessitated.
Notably, the feature maps outputted by each convolutional neu-
ral network module are essentially C dimensional vectors of 
size H ∗W, which exhibit a marked similarity to the structure 
of images or video frames. Given that the majority of terminal 
devices within edge computing networks are equipped with 
hardware-­accelerated video encoding and transmission capa-
bilities, this paper innovatively introduces a methodology for 
concatenating feature maps into video frames and subsequently 
encoding them for transmission. This approach significantly 
enhances data transmission efficiency and improves overall sys-
tem performance.
Initially, it is important to consider that the common hardware-­
accelerated encoding resolutions supported by terminal de-
vices, such as 720p, 1080p, and 4K, where the dimensions of 
the corresponding video frames are all multiples of 16. Hence, 
prior to feature map concatenation, a padding operation should 
be applied to the feature maps to adjust H and W to H′ and W ′ 
(where H′ and W ′ denote the nearest multiples of 16 to H and 
W, respectively). This ensures seamless concatenation of the 
feature maps. The method and number of feature map concat-
enations are determined based on the values of H′ and W ′, as 
well as the encoding parameters Penc supported by the terminal 
device hardware. The underlying principle of the concatenation 
process involves identifying an appropriate pair of positive inte-
gers m and n that satisfy (7) or (8): 
Subsequently, the feature maps are concatenated in accordance 
with the determined stitching pattern to generate video frames 
suitable for video encoding. Owing to the filtering process fa-
cilitated by the channel attention mechanism, the number of 
channels in the feature maps has been reduced from C to Cf. 
Consequently, it is possible that a complete video frame may not 
be fully formed during the concatenation process. To address 
this issue, it is imperative to append k blank frames of dimen-
sions H ∗W at the end. The value of k must satisfy (9). 
The “Efficient Data Transmission” in Figure 1 depicts an il-
lustrative process where the computation offloading point is 
selected after block b3 (when c3,4 = 1), and encoding and trans-
mission are conducted using 720P (1280 ∗ 720) video resolu-
tion. Initially, the feature maps, with dimensions 250 ∗ 75, will 
be padded with zeros around to adjust their size to 256 ∗ 80, 
ensuring they are multiples of 16. According to (7) or (8), 5 ∗ 9 
feature maps should be arranged within each video frame, 
and frames are concatenated sequentially until all feature 
maps are processed. Assume that 133 feature maps remain 
after feature map selection process, the last video frame will 
be not completely filled at this stage. Therefore, three blank 
feature maps, as determined by equation (9), are appended to 
form a complete video frame.
4.4   |   Efficient Data Transmission Scheme
The terminal device employs its integrated hardware encoding 
acceleration module to encode and transmit the video, resulting in 
a substantial reduction in data transmission time. Upon receiving 
the video frames from the device, the edge server decodes them 
and reconstructs the feature maps using video decoding algo-
rithms. Subsequently, it completes the remaining computational 
tasks to obtain the results of 3D object detection, which are then 
relayed back to the terminal device. To further enhance transmis-
sion efficiency, this paper utilizes the GStreamer media frame-
work to stream the hardware-­encoded video frames directly to 
the edge server. This approach significantly optimizes the encod-
ing and transmission process, minimizes read-­write interactions 
between the terminal device's memory and hard disk, and conse-
quently reduces the energy consumption of the terminal device.

we mentioned before, executing a single 3D detection task on 
Jetson TX2 takes over 5 s without external computational assis-
tance, which is not acceptable.
Assuming stable network conditions, the wireless router of-
fers a bandwidth of 16 Mbps for data transmission. The system 
employs a stereo camera to capture paired left and right im-
ages. Given the limited computational resources of terminal 
devices, we chose points after convolutional blocks 1, 2, and 
3 as our candidate offload points. We denote these points as 
cen,1,1 = 1, c1,2 = 1, c2,3 = 1, and c3,4 = 1, respectively. We utilize 
H.264 as the video encoding method. To thoroughly evaluate 
the performance, we conducted experiments on 3,769 pairs of 
images from the KITTI 3D Object Detection Dataset [27]. The 
KITTI dataset is a comprehensive collection of real-­world data 
for autonomous driving scenarios and contains a diverse range 
of objects such as cars, pedestrians, and cyclists, annotated with 
3D bounding boxes. The KITTI dataset classifies objects into 
three difficulty levels based on their size, occlusion, and trunca-
tion. The ‘Easy’ level comprises objects that are large, minimally 
occluded, and not truncated. The ‘Moderate’ level includes ob-
jects that are partially occluded or truncated. The ‘Hard’ level 
encompasses objects that are small, significantly occluded, or 
heavily truncated.

encoding on Jetson TX2. The edge server's responsibilities in-
clude (1) receiving video frame data, (2) decoding the video 
frames to reconstruct feature maps, (3) executing tasks after the 
offloading point, and (4) returning the detection results to the 
terminal devices.
The performance of our strategy is evaluated based on the fol-
lowing three key metrics: 
•	 Detection Time: The total time cost to obtain one detec-
tion result.
•	 Accuracy: Detection accuracy of the proposed strategy.
•	 Data Transmission Volume: The amount of data trans-
mitted to the server during a single detection process.
5.2   |   Comparison of Different Offloading Points
The backbone network ResNet-­101 utilized in this paper con-
sists of five convolutional modules. These modules' output 
positions can function as potential points for computation off-
loading. Given the limited computational resources of termi-
nal devices, we choose points after convolutional blocks 1, 2, 
and 3 as our candidate offload points. We denote these points 
as cen1,1 = 1, c1,2 = 1, c2,3 = 1 and c3,4 = 1, respectively. To thor-
oughly evaluate the performance, we conducted experiments on 
3,769 pairs of images. The size of each pair of images is around 
1806.3 KB. The results presented in Table 2 showcase the detec-
tion time achieved using different parameters, along with the 
corresponding transmission data volume for each candidate off-
loading point.
The above results indicate that all offloading strategies can ef-
fectively decrease detection time comparing with local execu-
tion on terminal devices. Moreover, the designed offloading 
strategies also offer substantial benefits over full offloading 
(cen1,1 = 1) by significantly reducing the amount of data trans-
mitted, which in turn lowers transmission time and conserves 
bandwidth, without imposing an undue burden on the device's 
processing capabilities. It is evident that the choice of the off-
loading point plays a crucial role in determining the overall sys-
tem performance.
Beyond evaluating detection time and data transmission vol-
ume, it is equally important to consider the detection accuracy.

6   |   Conclusion and Future Work
This paper introduces an efficient computation offloading and 
data transmission scheme tailored for 3D object detection algo-
rithms in edge computing networks. By taking into account both 
the computing and communication capabilities of terminal de-
vices and network conditions, our scheme achieves a balanced 
offloading of computational tasks, thereby alleviating the perfor-
mance requirements on terminal devices. Furthermore, through 
the integration of an attention-­based data transmission strategy 
and hardware-­coded acceleration, we effectively minimize data 
transmission latency and bandwidth consumption, ultimately 
enhancing the overall system performance. Experimental results 
demonstrate that our proposed scheme enables efficient 3D object 
detection while maintaining high detection accuracy, thus pro-
viding robust support for the deployment of 3D object detection 
technology on resource-­constrained devices. Given that our 3D 
object detection model utilizes the widely adopted ResNet net-
work as its backbone architecture, we believe that the strategies 
presented in this paper, with suitable modifications, can be ex-
tended to other computer vision algorithm applications.
Looking ahead, our goal is to further improve the processing 
speed and accuracy of our method. Additionally, we plan to 
refine and optimize our scheme for specific domains, such as 
connected vehicles and wireless sensor networks [28], with the 
aim of achieving asynchronous computation offloading and en-
abling multidevice collaborative computing capabilities.

Abstract: 3D object detection leverages sensors like LiDAR and cameras to capture scene information, enabling precise determination of objects' spatial positions and orientations. This technology finds extensive applications in autonomous driving, smart homes, in- dustrial automation, and intelligent security systems. However, high-­precision 3D object detection algorithms often require sub- stantial computational resources, posing limitations for deployment on resource-­constrained devices. In this paper, we devise an efficient computation offloading and data transmission framework specifically tailored for edge computing networks to address this challenge. Our framework takes into account both the computing and communication capabilities of terminal devices and network conditions, offloading suitable computation tasks to the edge for processing. This approach mitigates the algorithm's performance requirements on terminal devices. Furthermore, we propose a data transmission scheme that incorporates atten- tion mechanisms and hardware-­accelerated coding. This scheme effectively reduces detection time and enhances overall system performance. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed framework significantly enhances the efficiency of 3D object detection on resource-­constrained devices within edge computing networks, while maintaining high detection accuracy.
